items.content:
[This article was first published on r on Everyday Is A School Day, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

MICE always felt like magic to me So I tried rebuilding it from scratch in R to understand it better. Lots of mistakes and help along the way, but my version ended up close to the mice package. Might be just luck. Still learning, but here are my messy notes!

Motivations

We used mulitple imputation by chained equations (MICE) quite often in imputing missing data in many occasion, but I never really understood the mechanism behind it except that it appears magical! I want to see if I can build this from scratch as a mean to understand the foundation of MICE so that at least it will give me the illusion of understanding. Join me in my messy journey of trying to code it from the ground up (FYI, I’m not coding OLS or MLE from the ground up…), and let’s see if we can create some “magic” here! This is going to be a bumpy one with lots of coding, and maybe less of mathematical formulae. I’ll try my best to provide a TL;DR for each section so that we can get a high level view as well. Buckle up! And oh, Happy Halloween! What a better time to look at magical recipes of statistics! Let’s go!

Objectives:

  • What Is MICE
  • Simulate Our DGP
  • The Procedure To Impute And Create Multiple Datasets
    • Pool them!
  • Opportunities For Improvement
  • Lessons Learnt

What Is MICE

TL;DR: fill in each gap several times with plausible random guesses, analyse each completed dataset, then combine the results.

When data are missing, the tempting fix is to plug in one best guess, like the mean. The problem is that a single guess pretends we know the missing value exactly, so our standard errors come out too small. MICE takes a different approach: it fills in each missing value with a plausible random draw, and does this several times to create multiple complete datasets. The differences between those datasets capture our uncertainty about what the missing values really were.

The “chained equations” part is how those draws are made. Instead of one giant model for all variables at once, MICE fits a simple regression for each incomplete variable, using all the others as predictors, and cycles through them, each one feeding its freshly imputed values into the next. After a few rounds, the imputations settle down. Finally, we analyse each completed dataset and pool the results with Rubin’s rules.

Simulate Our DGP

Alright let’s simulate our data generating process (the truth) and add in missing data mechanism to create our dataset that we want to impute from (imagine this is the dataset that we have and we want to apply mice on it).

library(tidyverse)
library(broom)

set.seed(1)
n <- 1000
p1 <- rnorm(n)
p2 <- rnorm(n, 0.5*p1)
p3 <- rnorm(n, 0.4*p1 + 0.3*p2)
p4 <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
p5 <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.3*p1 - 0.2*p2 + 0.1*p3))
outcome <- rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-0.5 + 0.3*p1 - 0.2*p2 + 0.1*p3 + 0.5*p4 + 0.4*p5))

df <- tibble(p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,outcome)

# missing mechanism 
## mcar
p1_miss <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.1, NA, p1)
p3_miss <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.2, NA, p3)

## mar 
p2_miss <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-0.5 + 0.3*p1), NA, p2)
p4_miss <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-0.5 + 0.3*p1 - 0.2*p2), NA, p4)

## mnar
p5_miss <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-0.5 + 0.8*p5), NA, p5)

## recombine
df_miss <- tibble(p1 = p1_miss, p2 = p2_miss, p3 = p3_miss, p4 = p4_miss, p5 = p5_miss, outcome = outcome)

The Procedure To Impute And Create Multiple Datasets

Alright, let’s go through the procedure for MICE real quick.

  1. Index all missing values and record them in a dataframe.
  2. For each chain:
  • Fill every missing value with a random starting value.
  • For each column with missing data:
    • Bootstrap the rows where that column is observed, using the current filled-in values for the other columns.
    • Fit a model with that column as the response and all other columns, including the outcome, as predictors: linear regression for continuous columns, logistic for binary.
    • Predict the missing values, then add noise. For continuous columns, add a normal draw using the model’s residual SD. For binary columns, draw 0 or 1 from the predicted probability.
    • Write the new values back immediately, so the next column’s model uses them. This is the “chained” part.
  • Repeat the column loop for 10 iterations.
  • Keep the final imputed values from the 10th iteration.
  1. Repeat step 2 for 10 chains.
  2. Build 10 completed datasets, one per chain.
  3. Fit the analysis model on each dataset.
  4. Pool by averaging the coefficients, plus Rubin’s rules if you need standard errors.

Phew. What a procedure! At least we now know the machinery behind MICE!

Index all missing values and record them in a dataframe 

## procedure of simple mice
### 1. index all missing values
df_miss_idx <- df_miss |> is.na()

#### create an empty dataframe based on number of missing data
empty_row <- df_miss_idx |> as.vector() |> sum()

empty_df <- which(df_miss_idx, arr.ind = T) |> as_tibble()

data_type <- df_miss |> 
  map_chr(~class(.x)[1]) 

data_type_colnum <- 1:length(data_type)
colname <- colnames(df_miss)

data_type_df <- tibble(colnum = data_type_colnum, dtype=data_type, colname = colname)

empty_df <- empty_df |>
  left_join(data_type_df, by = c("col" = "colnum")) |>
  mutate(value = NA)

Notice that we added datatype to help us identify continuous data vs binary data?

Fill in missing values with random starting values

Let’s create a an empty dataframe then write functions to do these so we can use them on our for loop

### 2. First iteration, first chain
### 2a. randomly impute all values, use conditions per column to assess types of data before random normal, binomial distribution
fill_empty_df <- function(empty_df) { 
  df <- empty_df |>
  mutate(value = case_when(
    dtype == "numeric" ~ rnorm(n()),
    dtype == "integer" ~ rbinom(n(),1,0.5),
    TRUE ~ NA_real_
  )) |>
  mutate(model = case_when(
    dtype == "numeric" ~ "linreg",
    dtype == "integer" ~ "logreg",
    TRUE ~ NA_character_
  ))
  
  return(df)
}

grab_xvec <- function(df, outcome) {
  df |> 
    select(-all_of(outcome)) |>
    colnames()
}

gen_formula <- function(df, outcome) {
  x_vec <- grab_xvec(df, outcome)
  x <- paste(x_vec,collapse = "+")
  formula <- paste0(outcome,"~",x)
  return(formula)
}


formula_df <- empty_df |>
  distinct(colname, .keep_all = T) |>
  select(col, colname) |>
  mutate(formula = map(.x=colname, .f=~gen_formula(df_miss,.x)) |> unlist()) 


missing_fill <- function(empty_df) {
  df_miss_idx_fill <- matrix(nrow = nrow(df_miss), ncol = ncol(df_miss)) 
  
  for (i_mis in 1:empty_row) {
    rownum <- empty_df[[i_mis, "row"]]
    colnum <- empty_df[[i_mis, "col"]]
    data <- empty_df[[i_mis, "value"]]
    df_miss_idx_fill[rownum,colnum] <- data
  }
  
  df_miss_idx_fill <- df_miss_idx_fill |> as_tibble() 
  colnames(df_miss_idx_fill) <- colnames(df_miss)
  df_miss_idx_fill <- df_miss_idx_fill |>
    mutate(p4 = as.integer(p4),
           p5 = as.integer(p5))
  
  df_miss_df_miss_idx_fill <<- map2_dfc(df_miss, df_miss_idx_fill, coalesce) #learn about map2_dfc
}

empty_df contains randomly pulled number from respective datatype. grab_xvec grabs the predictor columns then gen_formula turns that into model formula for fitting. And missing_fill starts filling out the missing data Sorry if my code is not efficient. I’m sure we can have LLM make it even more efficient

Next, we iterate! 

# grab the colomuns that have missing values 
col_missing <- empty_df |> distinct(col) |> pull()

# create empty df so we can fill in
empty_df_mice <- tibble()
  
# set up chain
for (chain in 1:10) {
  
  # internally create another df so we can use and override data
  impute_df <- fill_empty_df(empty_df)
  
# for each chain iterate up to 10 times (this is where the chain equation starts)
for (iter in 1:10) {
  
# for each iteration look at each column with missing data
for (i in col_missing) {
  
  # refresh the filled dataset with the latest imputations
  missing_fill(impute_df)
  
  # set seed for each chain, iter, and column so that we can reproduce the same for testing purposes
  seed <- paste0(chain,iter,i) |> as.numeric()
  set.seed(seed)
  
  # look for datatype of the column we're evaluating now
  dtype <- impute_df |>
    filter(col == i) |>
    distinct(model)
  
  # a long winded way of sorting what columns to use for modeling and what to readd back
  empty_df_i <- impute_df |>
    filter(col == i)
  
  empty_df_i_not <- impute_df |>
    filter(col != i)
  
  # finding out what rows are missing and remove those for modelling
  missing_vec <- empty_df_i |>
    pull(row)
  
  df_miss_i_full <- df_miss_df_miss_idx_fill |>
    slice(-missing_vec)
  
  # resample (in place of posterior sampling)
  df_miss_i <- slice_sample(df_miss_i_full, replace = T, n = nrow(df_miss_i_full))
  
  
  # find out the formula for model
  formula <- formula_df |>
    filter(col == i) |>
    pull(formula)
  
  # algo for which estimator to use
  if (dtype == "linreg") {
  model_i <- lm(formula, data = df_miss_i)
  } 
  
  if (dtype == "logreg") {
   model_i <- glm(formula, data = df_miss_i, family = "binomial")   
  }

  newdata <- df_miss_df_miss_idx_fill |>
    slice(missing_vec)
  
  if (dtype == "logreg") {
  empty_df_i <- empty_df_i |>
    mutate(value = rbinom(nrow(empty_df_i), 1, predict(model_i, newdata = newdata, type = "response")))
  } else {
  empty_df_i <- empty_df_i |>
    mutate(value = predict(model_i, newdata = newdata) + rnorm(nrow(empty_df_i),0,sigma(model_i)))
  }
  
  impute_df <- empty_df_i_not |>
    rbind(empty_df_i)
  
}
  # only save the last iter data for each chain
  if (iter == 10) {
    empty_df_mice <- empty_df_mice |>
      rbind(impute_df |> mutate(chain = chain)) 
  }
  
}
}

# write a function to create dataframe based on chains
missing_fill_full <- function(x) {
  df_miss_idx_fill <- matrix(nrow = nrow(df_miss), ncol = ncol(df_miss)) 
  
  for (i_mis in 1:empty_row) {
    rownum <- x[[i_mis, "row"]]
    colnum <- x[[i_mis, "col"]]
    data <- x[[i_mis, "value"]]
    df_miss_idx_fill[rownum,colnum] <- data
  }
  
  df_miss_idx_fill <- df_miss_idx_fill |> as_tibble() 
  colnames(df_miss_idx_fill) <- colnames(df_miss)
  df_miss_idx_fill <- df_miss_idx_fill |>
    mutate(p4 = as.integer(p4),
           p5 = as.integer(p5))
  
  # merges both df and collapse those overlap completely
  map2_dfc(df_miss, df_miss_idx_fill, coalesce) 

}

# create 10 dataframes for each chain
for (data in 1:10) {
  df_miss_mice_i <- missing_fill_full(empty_df_mice |> filter(chain == data))
  assign(paste0("df_miss_mice_",data), df_miss_mice_i)
}

Wow, OK that’s a lot of code! Hopefully the comments above will be self-explainatory. Some of my code may be redundant. Now that we have 10 imputed dataset. The next recipe of the magic is fit each dataset to a model then pool them

Fit All! 

# put all 10 dataset into a list (probably should've done this before for efficienty, oh well)
imp_list <- map(.x=1:10, ~ missing_fill_full(empty_df_mice |> filter(chain == .x)))

# fit one at a time and save
fits <- map(imp_list, ~ glm(outcome ~ p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5,
                            data = .x, family = binomial))

Let’s take a peek at the first fit

fits[[1]] |> broom::tidy(conf.int = T)

Alright! Looks pretty ok.

Pool them 

# assess the point estimate of coefficient
coef <- 1:6
fit_list <- 1:10
temp_coef <- c()
# temp_coef_var <- c()
model_coef <- c()
model_coef_var <- c()
for (i in coef) {
  for (j in fit_list) {
  temp_coef[j] <- fits[[j]]$coefficients[[i]]
  }
  model_coef[i] <- mean(temp_coef)
  model_coef_var[i] <- var(temp_coef)
}

# assess the pooled SE to construct 95% CI of the coefficients
se <- do.call(rbind, map(.x = fits, ~ tidy(.x) |> pull(std.error))) |> as_tibble()
within_var <- colMeans(se^2) 
between_var <- model_coef_var 
total_var <- within_var + between_var + between_var / length(fit_list)
final_se <- sqrt(total_var)

# degrees of freedom (Barnard–Rubin)
lambda <- (1 + 1/length(fit_list)) * between_var / total_var
df_com <- 1000 - 6
df_old <- (length(fit_list) - 1) / lambda^2
df_obs <- (df_com + 1) / (df_com + 3) * df_com * (1 - lambda)
degfree <- df_old * df_obs / (df_old + df_obs)

tval <- qt(0.975, degfree)
mice_coef <- tibble(term = fits[[1]] |> tidy() |> pull(term), estimate = model_coef, std.error = final_se, tval = tval,
       conf.low = estimate - tval * std.error, conf.high = estimate + tval * std.error) |>
  select(-tval) |>
  mutate(method = "our_mice")

To combine our 10 models, we use Rubin’s rules. For the estimate, we just average the 10 coefficients. For the standard error, we add two kinds of uncertainty: the usual uncertainty within each model, and how much the 10 coefficients disagree with each other because of the missing data. Since that disagreement is estimated from only 10 datasets, we use a t value with Barnard–Rubin degrees of freedom instead of z score of 1.96 for 95% CI.

library(mice)

imp  <- mice(df_miss, m = 10, maxit = 10, seed = 1, printFlag = FALSE)
fit  <- with(imp, glm(outcome ~ p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5, family = binomial))
actual_mice_coef <- tidy(pool(fit), conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, std.error, conf.low, conf.high) |>
  mutate(method = "actual_mice")

For completeness sake, let’s use the professional’s method and see if our method matches up.

Grab All the Coefficients From Different Models 

## function to grab stats
grab_stats <- function(df, method) {
  model <- glm(outcome ~ p1 + p2 + p3 + p4 + p5, df, family = "binomial") 
  coef <- model |> tidy(conf.int = T) |> select(-statistic, -p.value) |> mutate(method = method)
  return(coef)
}

## full data
full_data_coef <- grab_stats(df, "full_data")

## complete case
cco_coef <- grab_stats(df_miss, "complete_case")

## complete case analysis
all_coef <- rbind(mice_coef, full_data_coef, cco_coef, actual_mice_coef)

## truth
truth <- tibble(term = c("(Intercept)", "p1", "p2", "p3", "p4", "p5"),
                truth = c(-0.5, 0.3, -0.2, 0.1, 0.5, 0.4))

## visualize all
all_coef |>
  ggplot(aes(x = estimate, y = term, color = method)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dotted", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_pointrange(aes(xmin = conf.low, xmax = conf.high),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
  geom_point(data = truth, aes(x = truth, y = term),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 4, size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Estimate (log-odds)", y = NULL,
       caption = "× = true coefficient") +
  theme_bw()

Our from-scratch MICE (purple) lines up closely with the mice package (red) for every coefficient, and both stay near the full-data fit (teal). Their intervals are slightly wider than the full-data ones, reflecting the extra uncertainty from the missing data. Complete-case analysis (green) drops every row with any missing value, so its estimates wander and its intervals are much wider. The × marks show the true coefficients from our data-generating process.

For p4, both MICE versions land a bit above the full-data estimate. Since they agree, it’s likely a quirk of this dataset rather than a coding problem. p5 is MNAR, yet both versions look fine here. That may just be luck in a single run, technically it shouldn’t really work, right?

Hooray! We did it! Wow, that was a long journey! I started this since 10/9/26 on the procedure, draft codes etc. Met lots of hurdles over the weeks. I’d be honest with you, it was bumpy! My initial go was a wrong approach where I average out the 10 datasets imputed data (which was wrong), then realized that that is not the proper pooling. Thanks to LLM being consistent tutor and back and forth conversaiton to converge to the proper technique. Now, I know how it works under the hood!

Opportunities For Improvement

  • next we should learn sampling from posterior instead of resampling
  • Try predictive mean matching, mice’s default. It borrows real observed values instead of adding normal noise, which keeps imputations within realistic ranges.
  • Make the code faster and tidier. Vectorise missing_fill(), keep everything in lists instead of global variables, and pass the random generator explicitly
  • try out sensitivity analysis with mice

Lessons learnt

  • learnt the machinery of mice!
  • learnt about map2_dfc
  • learnt about Barnard–Rubin degrees of freedom and how to pool using Rubin’s rule.
  • learnt total variance formula

items.title: Modelling cell-type proportions in repeated-measures designs with sccomp: a TMA case study
items.author: Stefano Mangiola
items.description:
Contributor: Pierre-Paul Axisa, Researcher, CBMR, Copenhagen, Denmark.
Introduction



Continue reading: Modelling cell-type proportions in repeated-measures designs with sccomp: a TMA case study
items.content:
[This article was first published on tidyomicsBlog, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here)
Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

Contributor: Pierre-Paul Axisa, Researcher, CBMR, Copenhagen, Denmark.

Introduction

Testing cell proportional differences from single-cell-resolved count data is central to modern tissue analyses. It becomes a repeated-measures problem as soon as several observations come from the same donor, such as multiple tumour cores in a tissue microarray (TMA) or serial biopsies over a time course. Averaging cores up to the patient and testing one phenotype at a time drops both the compositional constraint and the repeated-measures structure.

sccomp is a Bayesian model for mixed-effect compositional designs that identifies outliers probabilistically, tests for differential variability, and removes unwanted effects. It takes a long tibble with one row per sample and cell type, a count column, and the design columns, and sccomp_estimate(), sccomp_test(), and sccomp_predict() return tibbles ready for dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2.

Source study and study design

We apply sccomp to the NeoTRIP trial. Wang et al. (2023) used imaging mass cytometry (IMC) to map how multicellular spatial organization in triple-negative breast cancer relates to neoadjuvant immunotherapy response. In the phase III NeoTRIP trial (NCT02620280), early high-risk TNBC patients were randomised 1:1 to carboplatin + nab-paclitaxel (C) or the same regimen plus atezolizumab (C&I) for eight 3-week neoadjuvant cycles before surgery. Research FFPE biopsies:

  • Baseline (n = 243)
  • On-treatment (first day of cycle 2; n = 207)
  • Post-treatment (surgical excision; n = 210)
  • Profiled with a 43-marker IMC panel at subcellular resolution
  • Deep-learning segmentation and semi-supervised clustering defined 17 epithelial and 20 TME cell phenotypes
  • Multiple regions of interest (ROIs) were imaged per biopsy

Each patient contributes several samples. The biopsies are nested in the patient, and the regions of interest are nested in the biopsy. Patient NT193, in the chemotherapy arm with residual disease, was imaged at all three timepoints: 10 ROIs at baseline, 10 on-treatment, and 3 at surgery. In the model, each ROI is one compositional sample and the patient is the repeated-measures group.

One patient, three timepoints, several ROIs 
mk_spatial_tile <- function(dat, square = TRUE) {
  if (nrow(dat) == 0) {
    dat <- tibble::tibble(
      Location_Center_X = numeric(),
      Location_Center_Y = numeric(),
      draw = character()
    )
  }
  tile <- ggplot(dat, aes(x = Location_Center_X, y = Location_Center_Y)) +
    geom_point(data = filter(dat, draw == "other"), colour = "#39FF14", size = 0.10) +
    geom_point(data = filter(dat, draw == "pdl1"), colour = "#FFFF00", size = 0.16) +
    geom_point(data = filter(dat, draw == "m2"), colour = "#FF00FF", size = 0.16) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = NULL, guide = "none", expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_reverse(labels = NULL, guide = "none", expand = c(0, 0)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 8) +
    theme(
      plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", colour = NA),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "black", colour = NA),
      legend.position = "none",
      plot.margin = margin(
        if (square) 1 else 0, if (square) 1 else 0,
        if (square) 1 else 0, if (square) 1 else 0,
        unit = "pt"
      )
    )
  if (square) tile <- tile + theme(aspect.ratio = 1)
  tile
}

roi <- read_csv(
  file.path(results_dir, "sccomp_long_tme_immune_roi.csv"),
  col_select = c(PatientID, BiopsyPhase, ImageID),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(PatientID == "NT193") |>
  distinct() |>
  mutate(BiopsyPhase = factor(BiopsyPhase, phase_levels)) |>
  arrange(BiopsyPhase, ImageID) |>
  mutate(i = row_number(), .by = BiopsyPhase)

n_phase <- roi |>
  summarise(n = n(), .by = BiopsyPhase) |>
  mutate(x0 = cumsum(n + 2) - (n + 2))
roi <- roi |>
  left_join(n_phase, by = "BiopsyPhase") |>
  mutate(x = i + x0)

cells_nt <- read_fst(file.path(post_dir, "nt193-cells.fst")) |>
  as_tibble()
dx <- 0.46
pad <- 0.62
xmin <- min(roi$x) - pad
xmax <- max(roi$x) + pad
fig_w <- 12
fig_h <- 5.4
target_in <- (2 * dx) / (xmax - xmin) * fig_w
headroom <- 1.9
tile_h <- target_in * headroom / (fig_h - target_in)

phase <- roi |>
  summarise(x = mean(x), .by = BiopsyPhase) |>
  mutate(
    y = tile_h + 0.62,
    label = case_match(
      as.character(BiopsyPhase),
      "Baseline" ~ "Baseline\n10 ROIs",
      "On-treatment" ~ "On-treatment\n10 ROIs",
      "Post-treatment" ~ "Post-treatment\n3 ROIs"
    )
  )
patient <- tibble::tibble(
  x = mean(phase$x), y = phase$y[1] + 0.95, label = "Donor"
)
edges <- bind_rows(
  phase |> mutate(x, y, xend = patient$x, yend = patient$y),
  roi |> mutate(
    x,
    y = tile_h,
    xend = phase$x[match(BiopsyPhase, phase$BiopsyPhase)],
    yend = phase$y[1]
  )
)
phase_cols <- c(
  Baseline = "#1B9E77",
  `On-treatment` = "#D95F02",
  `Post-treatment` = "#7570B3"
)

tree <- ggplot() +
  geom_segment(
    data = edges, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_label(
    data = phase,
    aes(x, y, label = label, fill = BiopsyPhase),
    colour = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3, label.size = 0
  ) +

sccomp mixed-effects compositional modelling

Wang et al. summarised longitudinal composition as mean phenotype proportions per patient and compared arms, timepoints, and response groups with Wilcoxon tests, Z-scored trend plots (their Fig. 5), and per-phenotype weighted binomial GLMs on tumour-level proportions. Those tests treat each phenotype in isolation and average ROIs to the patient before inference, setting aside compositional closure (proportions sum to one) and the nesting of biopsies and ROIs within patients.

With sccomp, we model the ROI-level cell counts directly on a latent log-ratio scale with mixed effects on the mean and variability. Each ROI is one compositional sample (sample = "ROI_id" in sccomp_estimate()), several ROIs share a biopsy timepoint (BiopsyPhase), and a patient random intercept (1 | PatientID) accounts for baseline differences across individuals and shrinkage across the cohort:

sccomp analysis

The blocks below are the minimal tidyverse code to reproduce the analysis locally from the parsed input (run top to bottom), using the immune TME compartment with ROI-level samples and a patient random intercept.

From long-format tidy input

The input long is a tibble with one row per ROI × immune phenotype: ROI_id, a count, the design columns (Arm, BiopsyPhase, pCR), and the grouping PatientID. Several ROIs share one BiopsyPhase. Preview:

Hypothesis testing

We pass contrasts to sccomp_test() as strings.

marginal_CI_post compares responders with residual disease at that visit alone. Any gap the two groups already had at baseline is still in this result.

did_CI_post compares how far each group moved from its own baseline. A head start cancels, so the result is the difference in change.

Test two contrasts 
contrasts <- c(
  marginal_CI_post = paste(
    "`pCRpCR`",                                  # pCR versus RD in chemotherapy at baseline
    "`ArmC&I:pCRpCR`",                           # additional pCR versus RD gap in the C&I arm
    "`BiopsyPhasePost-treatment:pCRpCR`",        # additional pCR versus RD gap at post-treatment
    "`ArmC&I:BiopsyPhasePost-treatment:pCRpCR`", # additional pCR versus RD gap for C&I at post-treatment
    sep = " + "
  ),
  did_CI_post = paste(
    "`BiopsyPhasePost-treatment:pCRpCR`",        # change from baseline in the pCR contrast
    "`ArmC&I:BiopsyPhasePost-treatment:pCRpCR`", # further change from baseline in the C&I arm
    sep = " + "
  )
)

res <- sccomp_test(fit, contrasts = contrasts)

Predicted immune compositional trajectories

Figure 1 shows baseline-aligned predicted proportions (95% credible intervals) for all 15 immune TME phenotypes. Within each arm × cell-type facet, both response groups are shifted to the mean of their baseline predictions. Panels are split by treatment arm (columns); colour denotes pathological response. Asterisks mark arm–time points with difference-in-differences FDR < 0.05.

Align groups to a common baseline 
# Shift pCR and RD to their average baseline within each Arm x cell_group, per draw
shifts <- draws |>
  filter(BiopsyPhase == "Baseline") |>
  select(Arm, cell_group, .draw, pCR, proportion) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pCR, values_from = proportion) |>
  mutate(shift_pCR = (pCR + RD) / 2 - pCR,
         shift_RD  = (pCR + RD) / 2 - RD) |>
  select(Arm, cell_group, .draw, shift_pCR, shift_RD)

aligned_summary <- draws |>
  left_join(shifts, by = c("Arm", "cell_group", ".draw")) |>
  mutate(aligned_prop = proportion + if_else(pCR == "pCR", shift_pCR, shift_RD)) |>
  summarise(
    aligned_mean  = mean(aligned_prop),
    aligned_lower = quantile(aligned_prop, 0.025),
    aligned_upper = quantile(aligned_prop, 0.975),
    .by = c(Arm, BiopsyPhase, pCR, cell_group)
  )

  ) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = cols_response[["RD"]], mid = "white", high = cols_response[["pCR"]],
    midpoint = 0, limits = c(-lim, lim), name = "center_log_ratio"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Response-associated change from baseline (difference-in-differences)",
    x = NULL, y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_pub() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

Most of the signal is at post-treatment: 14 immune phenotypes have a significant DiD at post-treatment, and 9 on-treatment. For M2 Mac in the C&I arm, the on-treatment DiD FDR is 0.21 and the post-treatment DiD FDR is 0.007. The on-treatment marginal contrast largely repeats a baseline difference.

M2 macrophage changes by response

Figure 3 compares pCR versus residual disease at each visit with the change from baseline. Points above the dotted line are FDR < 0.05.

M2 macrophage changes by response 
m2_volcano <- bind_rows(
  hmc_marginal_pcr |>
    filter(cell_group == "M2 Mac") |>
    mutate(Arm, BiopsyPhase, c_effect, c_FDR, family = "Marginal pCR vs RD"),
  hmc_did |>
    filter(contrast_family == "did", cell_group == "M2 Mac") |>
    mutate(Arm, BiopsyPhase, c_effect, c_FDR, family = "DiD (change from T0)")
) |>
  mutate(label = paste(Arm, BiopsyPhase, sep = " · "))

ggplot(m2_volcano, aes(x = c_effect, y = -log10(pmax(c_FDR, 1e-12)))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = 2, colour = "grey70") +
  geom_point(aes(colour = family, shape = BiopsyPhase), size = 2.8) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 2.3, vjust = -0.9, colour = "grey25") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(
    "Marginal pCR vs RD" = "#999999",
    "DiD (change from T0)" = "#d73027"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "M2 Mac: visit contrast and change from baseline",
    x = "center_log_ratio",
    y = expression(-log[10](FDR)),
    colour = NULL, shape = NULL
  ) +
  theme_pub()

Between-patient heterogeneity in M2 Mac

The fixed effect is the population estimate. Patient random intercepts describe individual baselines and trajectories. Figure 4 shows the per-patient predicted M2 Mac trajectories.

Between-patient M2 trajectories 
pred_pat <- hmc_pred_patient |>
  filter(cell_group == "M2 Mac") |>
  mutate(cell_group = factor(cell_group))

pcr_cols <- c("RD" = "#4575b4", "pCR" = "#d73027")

ggplot(pred_pat, aes(x = BiopsyPhase, y = proportion_mean, group = PatientID, colour = pCR)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  facet_grid(cell_group ~ Arm + pCR, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = pcr_cols, name = "Response") +
  labs(
    title = "Between-patient variation in predicted M2 Mac proportion",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Predicted proportion"
  ) +
  theme_pub() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", strip.text = element_text(size = 8))

Visualise results in spatial context

Figure 2 identifies two C&I post-treatment phenotypes that move in opposite directions by response: M2 Mac increases more from baseline in pCR (DiD FDR 0.007), whereas PD-L1+APCs decreases (DiD FDR 0.000). Figure 5 plots both markers on the tissue for 20 representative patients per response group (those closest to each group’s median post-treatment M2 proportion), showing all post-treatment ROIs per patient (pCR left, RD right; magenta = M2 Mac, yellow = PD-L1+APCs, green = other immune TME).

Spatial maps of post-treatment cores 
cores <- read_csv(file.path(post_dir, "spatial-cores.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
cells <- read_fst(file.path(post_dir, "spatial-cells.fst")) |> as_tibble()

mk_roi <- function(image_id) {
  if (is.na(image_id)) return(patchwork::plot_spacer())
  mk_spatial_tile(filter(cells, ImageID == image_id))
}

mk_row <- function(pid) {
  image_ids <- cores |>
    filter(PatientID == pid) |>
    arrange(roi) |>
    pull(ImageID)
  ids <- c(image_ids, rep(NA_character_, 3L - length(image_ids)))
  patchwork::wrap_plots(
    ggplot() +
      annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 0.5, label = pid, fontface = "bold", size = 2.8) +
      scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
      scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1), expand = c(0, 0)) +
      theme_void(),
    patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(ids, mk_roi), nrow = 1, ncol = 3),
    ncol = 1,
    heights = c(0.16, 1)
  )
}

mk_block <- function(response, title) {
  one_column <- function(which_side) {
    pids <- cores |>
      filter(pCR == response, side == which_side) |>
      arrange(patient) |>
      distinct(PatientID) |>
      pull(PatientID)
    patchwork::wrap_plots(lapply(pids, mk_row), ncol = 1)
  }
  patchwork::wrap_plots(one_column("left"), one_column("right"), ncol = 2) +
    patchwork::plot_annotation(
      title = title,
      theme = theme(
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12, hjust = 0.5, margin = margin(b = 4))
      )
    )
}
